entities.name: Pausanias of Orestis
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Pausanias of Orestis, a member of Philip II of Macedon's elite personal bodyguard (somatophylakes), holds a pivotal, albeit brief, place in ancient history as the assassin who brought an abrupt end to the reign of one of antiquity's most formidable unifiers in 336 BCE. Hailing from the Macedonian region of Orestis, his act at Aegae, the ancient capital, irrevocably altered the trajectory of the Hellenistic world, directly paving the way for the meteoric rise of Alexander the Great. His significance lies not in his own deeds beyond this singular act, but in the monumental shift of power and the subsequent imperial expansion that his actions unleashed.

The assassination occurred during the lavish wedding celebration of Philip's daughter Cleopatra to Alexander I of Epirus, a grand public spectacle intended to reinforce Macedonian power and alliances. As Philip processed into the theatre, Pausanias fatally stabbed him. Ancient historians, notably Diodorus Siculus and Justin, attribute Pausanias's motive to a personal grievance: a perceived slight and sexual assault committed against him by Philip's father-in-law Attalus, which Philip allegedly failed to adequately punish. This deeply personal vendetta, possibly inflamed by political machinations within the Macedonian court, culminated in the regicide. Pausanias was immediately pursued by Philip's bodyguards and killed during his escape, leaving many questions about potential co-conspirators unanswered.
